DA3021 · Course Project · IIT Guwahati · Monsoon 2026

Brightness Is Not
Information

Can AI see what the camera never captured? A camera throws information away in at least three places. AI fills all three back in, convincingly. Using live demos and real experiments with Real-ESRGAN on real photographs, this page measures where the measuring stops and the guessing begins.

Banoth Sree Ram Nayak · Roll No. 240150007 · IIT Guwahati
How to use this page. Every section has a short claim, a live demo or a real result, and a takeaway. Grey buttons switch between images, and sliders change settings live. Everything runs inside your browser: no internet and no server needed, and no image you upload leaves your computer.

00 · Motivation · VIP Module 1 (the eye)

You are about to hallucinate

Each of your eyes has a patch with no photoreceptors at all, where the optic nerve leaves. You have never seen a hole there, because your brain fills it with a guess.

+
  1. Close your left eye. Look straight at the + with your right eye.
  2. Move slowly toward the screen, then away (around 30–60 cm).
  3. At one distance the red dot vanishes, and the stripes look continuous where it was.

Your brain did not see stripes there. It invented them from the surroundings. The rest of this page asks the same question about cameras and AI: how much of what we "see" was measured, and how much was guessed?

01 · VIP Module 1: the Bayer filter

Two-thirds of every photo is a guess

A camera pixel measures only one colour, red, green or blue, through a tiny filter. The other two values at every pixel are interpolated from the neighbours.

33.3%
values measured
66.7%
values guessed
–
mean error (guessed)
–
false colour added

How to read this: the 2nd panel is the raw sensor. Every pixel is only red, green or blue, so it looks like a green chessboard. The 3rd panel fills in the two missing colours at every pixel by averaging neighbours. The 4th panel shows the error, brightened 4×: black means the guess was right, and bright means the guess was wrong. Try Grey zone plate: the truth has no colour at all, so every colour in panel 3 is invented.

Real photo · OpenCV demosaicing algorithms

With the grey zone plate, the true image has no colour at all, so every colour in the demosaiced result was invented. On a real photo, interpolation does well on smooth fur but fails on thin whiskers. The guesses break exactly where the fine detail, and therefore the information, was.

02 · VIP Module 1: cones & metamers

Two different lights, one identical photo

A spectrum here is 31 numbers (400–700 nm). The camera reduces it to 3. That leaves 28 directions of change the camera cannot see at all, and no algorithm applied afterwards can recover them.

Surface A Surface B Light shaded: camera R, G, B sensitivity
A
B
–
camera RGB · A
–
camera RGB · B
–
max difference
B − A: a change that lives entirely in the camera's null space

How to read this: the black and red curves are how much light two surfaces reflect at each wavelength. The shaded hills are how sensitive the camera's R, G and B pixels are. The camera multiplies each curve by each hill and adds up, so it keeps 3 numbers out of 31. Surface B was built so that those three sums come out identical, which is why the swatches match under white light. Change Lighting to an RGB LED or a sodium lamp and the swatches split, because the light changed which wavelengths count.

Under white light, A and B give exactly the same RGB values (difference 0/255) for every pair you generate. Under an RGB LED or a sodium lamp they split by tens of levels (for the pair in my slides: 57/255 and 65/255). The information existed in the world but never reached the photo, so no AI can recover it. Your eyes have the same limit: three cone types also collapse each spectrum to three numbers.

03 · VIP Module 2: the 2-D Fourier transform

Shrinking an image deletes part of its spectrum

Downsample by a factor f and every spatial frequency outside the dashed box is gone. Classical upscaling cannot put anything back, because it has nothing to put back.

–
energy outside box · original
–
energy outside box · upscaled

How to read this: the coloured squares are the 2-D Fourier transform (VIP Module 2). The centre holds coarse patterns, the edges hold fine detail, and brighter means more of that pattern. The shrunk image can only hold the frequencies inside the dashed box; everything outside it is fine detail that no longer exists. With bicubic, the outside of the second spectrum is almost dark. With nearest, the blocky pixel edges create high frequencies of their own: that is false detail too, just an ugly kind, which is why bicubic is the fair baseline.

Turn off anti-aliasing on the zone plate and the lost high frequencies don't just vanish: they fold back as false rings (aliasing). The spectrum shows plainly what was measured and what was not, and the next section uses that test on a real AI.

Before the results · how to read the numbers

Six terms used in every result

Shrink ×4

The 256×256 photo is reduced to 64×64. That keeps 1 pixel in 16, and this small image is all either method gets to see.

Bicubic

A classic formula that enlarges by smooth interpolation. It uses no training data, so it cannot add detail. It is the honest baseline.

Real-ESRGAN

A widely used AI upscaler (Wang et al., 2021), a neural network trained with a GAN to produce realistic-looking detail. It ran here with its official weights.

PSNR (dB)

Peak signal-to-noise ratio: how close an image is, pixel by pixel, to the real photo. Higher is closer to the truth. A 3 dB drop means the average squared error has doubled.

Energy outside the box

The share of the image's Fourier energy beyond what a 64×64 input can hold (the dashed box). Anything there was added, not measured.

Match with true detail

The correlation (−1 to 1) between the added high-frequency detail and the detail that was really lost. 1 means right, 0 means unrelated.

04 · The experiment · Real-ESRGAN on real photographs

Sharper to the eye, further from the truth

Each photo was shrunk ×4 and then enlarged back two ways: by bicubic interpolation, which adds nothing, and by Real-ESRGAN, a widely used generative upscaler. The comparison uses the original photo as ground truth.

Real photos (CC0 / public domain) · official Real-ESRGAN x4plus weights

How to read this: top row: the truth, what the methods were given, and the two answers. Bottom row: their Fourier spectra (dashed box = what the input can hold) and a map of what the AI drew that bicubic did not. Switch photos with the buttons above. Red values in the table are the AI's.

On every one of the four photos, Real-ESRGAN puts energy back outside the box (cat: 2.3% vs 0.04% for bicubic) yet ends up with a lower PSNR than plain bicubic (cat: 26.0 vs 28.5 dB). On the brick wall it adds more high-frequency energy than the real photo had (24.6% vs 8.8%). That energy correlates with the true lost detail only where the texture is regular and predictable (brick, wood grain), and hardly at all for unique detail such as whiskers. It looks sharper, but it is more confident, not better informed.

05 · The telephone game

Ask the AI to remember, six times

Shrink the photo ×4, let Real-ESRGAN enlarge it, then repeat with its own output. Each round, the only new information comes from the model's training data, never from the scene.

Real photo · Real-ESRGAN x4plus, 6 rounds

PSNR (dB)correlation with true high band (0–0.2)

PSNR falls from 26.0 to 19.2 dB, and the match with the real fine detail falls from 0.13 to 0.05. The high-frequency energy keeps rising. The image drifts toward what the model "likes": smooth surfaces, hard outlines and invented colours. The blue in the eyes was never in the photo.

06 · VIP Module 1: photon noise

Same scene, eight photos, eight different "details"

Take eight photos of the same scene. They differ only by sensor noise (σ = 2% of full brightness, about 5/255). If the AI's detail were truly in the scene, all eight outputs would agree.

Real photo · 8 noisy captures · Real-ESRGAN x4plus
5.4/255
95th-pct variation · bicubic
8.1/255
95th-pct variation · AI

For bicubic, the noise spreads evenly and without structure. For the AI, the variation concentrates on the eyes, the whisker pads and the edges, exactly where it adds "detail". Part of what looks like detail is the model's response to noise. This is a map of where the camera's information ran out.

07 · Nyquist + noise, in the real world

"Enhance!" One blur, many truths

Information is a difference you can measure above the noise, not brightness. If two different number plates produce nearly the same blurry image, the photo does not contain the plate.

Real-ESRGAN x4plus on rendered plates
True plate "AS01 GK 4721"
True plate "A501 GK 4721"
Ground truth
Shrunk ×8 → AI
Shrunk ×12 → AI

At ×8 the AI reads both plates correctly. At ×12 two different plates give practically the same output: confident, sharp-edged and wrong. The AI is no longer reading the plate, because the information is no longer there.

Try it live
The truth (sharp)
What the camera recorded
Can the photo tell?

How to use: type any plate, then use New look-alikes to swap in confusable characters (0/O/D, 1/7/I, 5/S, 8/B). Lower the shrink or the noise and the verdicts turn green, because the information comes back. SNR is the total difference between the blurred images divided by the sensor noise; below about 3, no method can reliably tell the plates apart.

The verdict uses a signal-to-noise ratio: the total difference between each look-alike's blurred image and the true one, divided by the sensor noise. When it drops below about 3, the photo cannot separate the plates, but an AI will still output a sharp one.

08 · SAP Modules 1, 3 & 6: spectrogram, source–filter, codecs

The same thing happens in sound

A phone line keeps only frequencies up to about 3.4 kHz. Codecs then rebuild the missing highs by copying the band below (spectral band replication). It sounds brighter, but the highs are invented.

Source–filter synthesis (SAP Module 3) · 16 kHz
Original
Telephone band
Highs "replicated"

How to read this: a spectrogram (SAP Module 1) shows time across and frequency up, and brighter means louder. The five sounds are /a/, /i/, /u/, /s/ and /f/, made with a source–filter model (SAP Module 3): a buzz shaped by vocal-tract resonances. The dashed line is the 3.4 kHz phone cutoff. Use headphones to hear the difference.

Above 3.4 kHz, the original /s/ is louder than /f/ (55 vs 47 dB). After band replication the order flips (15 vs 33 dB). The /s/ lived almost entirely above the cutoff, so nothing was left to copy from. This is the old telephone s/f confusion, and it is why people spell "S for Sugar" over the phone. It is the same failure as the plate: the guess is plausible and wrong.

09 · Try it on your own AI output

The hallucination meter

Upload an image enlarged by any AI upscaler. The page measures how much spectral energy the AI placed outside the box that the low-res input could contain. That energy came from the model's training data, not from your photo.

How to use: enlarge any small photo ×4 with an AI upscaler (for example an online "AI image upscaler" or Real-ESRGAN), then upload the result as 1 and, if you have it, the small original as 2. The meter compares the AI against bicubic from the same pixels. A hallucination ratio far above 1 means most of the fine detail was generated, not measured.

Spectra use a Hann window. Without the low-res input, the baseline is made by shrinking the AI output by the factor, which assumes the AI kept the input's coarse content. That assumption is usually close to true.

10 · Reflection

Who is guessing?

Partly recoverable

Bayer mosaic

Natural images are smooth, so guesses from neighbours are usually right. They fail exactly on fine detail.

Gone, filled by priors

Beyond Nyquist

Frequencies above the sampling limit are not in the data. AI fills them with what similar images usually contain, which works for bricks and fails for whiskers and number plates.

Gone for good

Metamers

The camera's null space. Two worlds produce identical numbers, and no prior can separate them.

You, too

Your eye

A cone mosaic, a blind spot and a blurry periphery. Your brain demosaics, fills in and upscales all day.

The camera, the AI and your brain all guess. What matters is whether the guess is honest about being a guess.

How the results were made

The real experiments ran Real-ESRGAN with its official released weights (RealESRGAN_x4plus.pth, xinntao/Real-ESRGAN v0.1.0) through a NumPy re-implementation of its RRDBNet architecture. All code and the raw numbers (assets/results.json) are in the code/ folder of this site's repository, so anyone can re-run them. Degradation was bicubic ×4 with anti-aliasing. Metrics were computed on 256×256 crops with a Hann window. Demosaicing used OpenCV (bilinear, VNG, edge-aware). The audio was synthesised with a source–filter model, not recorded.
